summary:
Blink X is a web application for exploring and analyzing multi-epoch near-infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users enter coordinates or resolve astronomical targets via SIMBAD and NED to inspect sky patches across observation dates using blink animation, image subtraction and addition, and 3D hyperspectral cube slicing across all six detectors and 102 spectral channels (0.75–5.00 µm).

The platform addresses the challenge of spotting faint or fast-moving objects among SPHEREx’s massive all-sky datasets by combining visual time-comparison tools with Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalog overlays, contamination flag filtering, interactive molecular spectra, and proper-motion or JPL Horizons asteroid trajectory predictions. Researchers and citizen scientists can also log timestamped notes, share exact view states via URL, and export astrometric reports in IAU ADES-PSV format.

Because SPHEREx maps over a billion objects every six months, manual inspection of raw archives is impractical. Blink X turns multi-band infrared releases into an accessible browser workspace where anyone can detect brown dwarfs, asteroids, and variable stars.
details:
What is Blink X and How Does It Work? Blink X is a web application built to explore and analyze multi-epoch near-infrared observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Inspired by the classic blink comparator used to spot moving objects across the night sky, the platform automates the retrieval, alignment, and inspection of multi-band infrared data directly in the browser.

Users enter sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination in decimal or sexagesimal format) or search astronomical targets by name through SIMBAD and NED. Blink X then loads the available observation dates for that sky patch and lets users animate through epochs, subtract or add images (T2 - T1 and T1 + T2) to isolate movement or brightness changes, and slice through 3D hyperspectral cubes across all six SPHEREx detectors (D1-D6) and 102 spectral channels (0.75 to 5.00 µm). Clicking any pixel opens a point probe that plots the local spectrum, highlights molecular absorption bands (H2O, CH4, CO2, CO, NH3), and filters out contaminated pixels.

Key Features and Practical Benefits

  • Multi-epoch blink, subtraction, and stacking: Users can toggle between observation dates or generate difference and summed images on the fly to detect high-proper-motion stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids, and variable stars without manually downloading or reprojecting FITS files.
  • 102-channel spectral and detector inspection: The viewer separates data by detector array and wavelength, allowing users to inspect individual spectral slices, view RGB composites, and analyze chemical signatures.
  • Catalog cross-matching and motion prediction: Blink X overlays sources from Gaia DR3 and AllWISE over the field of view to distinguish known background stars from moving candidates. It also projects proper-motion trajectories and queries JPL Horizons to predict asteroid positions across time windows ranging from six hours to 30 days.
  • Field notes, URL sharing, and scientific exports: An integrated observation log saves timestamped notes tied to exact sky coordinates, field of view, and detector settings. Users can share reproducible views via URL parameters, download channel images as PNGs, export observation logs in Markdown, or generate astrometric reports in standard IAU ADES-PSV format.
  • Interactive onboarding and offline fallback: A chapter-based landing page with a blink mini-game introduces how multi-epoch detection works before users enter the main explorer. When external archives are slow or unavailable, a local dataset mode keeps core inspection tools usable.

Intended Impact SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, producing data on more than a billion objects. No single research team can visually inspect that volume of multi-epoch imagery alone. Blink X removes the software setup and file-handling barriers of raw astronomical archives so both researchers and citizen scientists can inspect real SPHEREx fields, verify moving candidates, and contribute reproducible observations from a standard web browser.

Tools, Tech Stack, and Data Sources Team Hextech built Blink X with a decoupled frontend and backend architecture:

  • Frontend: Astro, React, TypeScript, HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript, using Recharts for interactive spectral and time-series plots and custom canvas rendering for tangential (TAN) sky projections.
  • Backend and Processing: Python 3 with FastAPI and Uvicorn, supported by Astropy, Reproject, and Astroquery for coordinate transforms, FITS handling, and archive queries, alongside NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Pillow, and Matplotlib for image processing. HTTPX, Requests, Pydantic, and DiskCache manage asynchronous requests and local caching.
  • Machine Learning and Optimization: Detection and scoring models were prototyped in Jupyter Notebooks using PyTorch and Scikit-learn, then exported to ONNX and ONNX Runtime for fast server-side inference.
  • Astronomical Data Services: Blink X integrates live queries to NASA/IPAC IRSA, IVOA Simple Image Access (SIA), ESA Gaia DR3, NASA/JPL Horizons, NASA/IPAC NED, CDS SIMBAD, and CDS Sesame.
  • Development Workflow: We used Bash scripts and pytest for automation and testing, and used AI coding assistants (Claude and ChatGPT) during development to debug astronomical coordinate conversions and structure documentation.

Creativity and Key Considerations Blink X pairs a century-old visual astronomy technique with hyperspectral infrared cubes, interactive molecular filtering, and browser-based astrometric reporting. Instead of limiting users to static cutouts or command-line scripts, the interface lets anyone move smoothly between a guided educational introduction and a full scientific workstation.

During development, our team prioritized three practical constraints:

  • Accessibility: Hiding FITS reprojection, WCS alignment, and multi-detector indexing behind coordinate search and one-click presets for benchmark targets such as Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.
  • Performance: Using asynchronous job polling, DiskCache, ONNX Runtime, and preloaded local fields so large multi-epoch queries stay responsive.
  • Scientific rigor: Surfacing contamination flags, error bars, detector metadata, and cross-matched Gaia and WISE catalogs so every visual candidate can be verified against existing astronomical records.
